principle: Make everything players must read stand out from decoration
why: In an action game players must always know where solid ground, opponents and threats are, and a perspective 3D view makes collision hard to recognize. Elaborate backdrops easily steal attention; his standing note to stage artists is that the backdrop is outshining the terrain. He still wants the stage to look good, because visuals sell the game, so gameplay gets the slight edge rather than total victory.
how_to_apply: Highlight every collision surface in a debug view and check it reads at a glance in the normal view. Push non-colliding scenery back with aerial perspective and weaker contrast, then repair the overall look. Check that platforms, projectiles, costumes and fighters in shadow or vignetting stay visible, and that the floor doesn't overpower projectiles. Desaturate screenshots to see what actually stands out. Give dangerous attacks a visual tell players can react to.
anti_pattern: A backdrop that outshines the terrain. Drop-through platforms, costumes or fighters that vanish into dark or busy scenes. Fixing readability only by fogging out the background until the stage looks bad.
example: Smash stage reviews with collision marked in red; Mishima Dojo fighters in shadow checked with a desaturated image; Hollow Bastion's floor toned down so Greninja's Water Shuriken stays visible; the P8 Enderman costume pitched as a game of 'find the Enderman'; Punch-Out!!'s yellow eyes as a dodge cue.
review_question: In a grayscale screenshot of a busy moment, are terrain, characters, platforms and projectiles the most prominent things on screen?
keywords: readability clarity legibility terrain collision backdrop background foreground contrast aerial-perspective visibility platforms projectiles telegraph tells

principle: Keep characters visible inside their own effects
why: Effects are needed for impact, but characters easily get lost in a sea of them. In 2D you can draw characters above effects; in 3D, forcing characters to draw on top creates depth disparity and looks wrong, and lowering the effect's priority instead can leave you seeing only terrain. So the fix has to live in the shape of the effect itself.
how_to_apply: Review each big effect with the character inside it at gameplay camera angles. Leave gaps around the body. Make the parts of a surrounding effect that sit between camera and character lower than the parts behind it. Add an outline to character models. Cut layered effects or background atmosphere that bury fighters, and make scattering elements like hit stars fly far enough not to hide behind bodies.
anti_pattern: Forcing 3D characters to render on top of effects. Lowering hit-mark draw priority until terrain hides them. Layered throw effects or super-move backdrops that hide the fighters.
example: Terry stays clear inside Power Dunk's crown effect; Falcon Punch keeps Captain Falcon partly visible; the inner peaks of Chrom's Up Special differ in height seen from front and back; Sora's down-throw effects were thinned because they hid the fighters.
review_question: Pause on the biggest effect each character makes: can you still see the character's pose?
keywords: effects occlusion draw-priority display-priority outline characters visibility buried sea-of-effects vfx aura

principle: Never let color alone carry gameplay meaning
why: If a game is built mainly around color, players with color blindness can't play it, because certain hues look alike to them. The same problem hits power-ups and interactive stage objects in any genre, not just puzzle games. He treated this as essential before he could call Meteos complete.
how_to_apply: Run screenshots of every color-coded element through a color-blindness simulation filter (Photoshop includes one). Where hues merge, separate them by brightness, not just hue, without making them so dark they vanish into the background. Also check whole screens in black and white. Keep each screen to one dominant color theme rather than a mishmash.
anti_pattern: Puzzle pieces, pickups or team markers told apart by hue only. Darkening pieces until they disappear against the background. A jumble of competing colors on one screen.
example: Meteos blocks checked with a protanopia filter and redesigned with significant brightness differences while staying visible on each planet's background.
review_question: Through a color-blindness filter and in grayscale, can every gameplay-critical element still be told apart?
keywords: color-blindness colorblind accessibility protanopia deuteranopia brightness value hue color-coding grayscale black-and-white

principle: Give every character a silhouette that reads even in solid black
why: Of the ways he knows to make an imaginary character look cool, the silhouette is the one he stresses most. Characters are often small on screen and seen from one main angle, so an ambiguous outline, or one that resembles another character, fails. Exaggerated shapes are also what establish a character, as with Nakoruru's hair and ribbon or Sonic's big head and skinny limbs.
how_to_apply: Fill each character and key pose in solid black and compare the whole cast side by side. Exaggerate signature features (hair, ribbons, gloves, head size, limb thickness). Check key poses from the game's main viewpoint, with all four limbs readable and on both sides of the screen. Brighten extremities such as hands, feet or socks so movement reads. Sharpen shapes that have gone soft.
anti_pattern: Realistic proportions that blur together at game size. Two characters with near-identical outlines. Symmetric, front-facing poses that hide the limbs.
example: Nakoruru's emphasized hair, ribbon, gloves and legs; Sonic's head and limbs; the Mii maid outfit's socks colored white so movement reads; Devil Kazuya's too-rounded wing silhouette sharpened; Sora's back jump given a more energetic silhouette.
review_question: Filled in solid black, is each character's form exaggerated, readable and impossible to confuse with anyone else?
keywords: silhouette shape-language character-design readability outline exaggeration solid-black extremities poses distinct cast

principle: Give effects contrast with crisp shapes and dark accents, not glow alone
why: Additive blending adds an element's colors to the background, pushing it toward white. Layering it gives decent results from simple visuals, 'but that's it': the effect lacks impact and contrast, can be too bright, and vanishes on light backgrounds. Keeping the whole game dark to show effects off still falls short. Opposing elements make any image stand out, like straight lines in a curvy design.
how_to_apply: Build each effect around solid polygons or simple images as the focal point, with additive glow as support. Mix dark elements (black accents, a dark backdrop behind a hit mark) into bright effects. Test every effect on your brightest and darkest backgrounds. When processing is tight, mixing white and black pixels makes an effect show on any color.
anti_pattern: Effects made only of bright additive layers. Darkening the whole game so effects show. Low-contrast effects that disappear on white or bright stages.
example: Smash Ultimate builds all its effects around crisp shapes for a clean, anime-style look; Sora's Blizzaga got dark elements because it vanished on bright stages; Kirby's Dream Land's inhale effect mixed white and black pixels.
review_question: On the game's brightest background, does every effect still pop with a clear shape and contrast?
keywords: vfx effects additive-blending contrast pop dark-elements black crisp shapes polygons anime glow bright-background

principle: Fit each hit mark to its hit: size, place, layers and duration
why: Hit marks exist for clear visual feedback and fun, so they should be flashy in proportion to the impact. They must appear where the attack and target hitboxes actually met or they look wrong, which a pulled-back camera with large hitboxes makes tricky. Quick repeated hits need short marks, and even big ones should resolve fairly quickly. Hitstop gives the mark extra time to animate.
how_to_apply: Scale size and flashiness by attack strength. Spawn the mark at the real contact point and check placement in game. Layer a main flash, a shockwave behind the target, an upward spray and material extras such as sparks for machines, without clutter. Keep durations short, shortest for rapid hits. Let the mark keep animating during hitstop while the characters freeze. Adapt any borrowed effect to your own camera distance and hit frequency.
anti_pattern: One generic spark for every hit. Marks floating where nothing connected. Lingering effects that pile up. Cartoony marks pasted unchanged onto realistic subjects. Copying a lavish effect from a game with different hardware, camera distance or hit rates.
example: Smash Ultimate's hit marks with shockwaves, upward sprays, sparks on mechanical opponents and dark backdrops; the hitstop effect that shows the flight path the hit player can slightly adjust; Sora's hit stars sent flying farther so they don't vanish behind Donkey Kong.
review_question: Does each hit mark's size and length match the hit, appear exactly where it connected, and clear before the next hit?
keywords: hit-marks hit-effects hit-sparks impact feedback contact-point hitbox hitstop layering duration vfx combat

principle: Flash for impact and status, with internal contrast and fixed color meanings
why: A full-screen flash adds impact the way screen shake does, because it covers a large area; a character flash emphasizes a change in that character's status, and he calls both crucial. Adding white or one color evenly lowers contrast, since the same amount goes onto dark and light areas and they average out, and a white flash makes the character vanish on light backgrounds.
how_to_apply: Add shadows or dark elements into hit flashes so the character keeps internal contrast. Give each status one flash color or treatment and keep it consistent. Use rim lighting to signal states like invulnerability. Scale flash strength with camera distance so close-ups don't flash most of the screen. Keep flashes to a single brief moment and full-screen flashes mild. Check them on real LCDs, whose response time changes how they look.
anti_pattern: Flashing a character pure white. One flash color meaning several things. Full-strength flashing when the camera is zoomed in.
example: Smash Ultimate's shadowed hit flash, built from a mockup Sakurai drew; white flash for invulnerability while getting up; yellow flash for the window after a throw when the character can't be grabbed again; rim lighting for damage types; Kirby's Adventure freezing and flashing the screen when a boss falls.
review_question: Can a player name what each character flash means, and does a flashing character stay readable on a light background?
keywords: flash flashing hit-flash white-flash screen-flash status invulnerability rim-lighting internal-contrast boss-stop photosensitivity

principle: Treat effects as essential and study them frame by frame
why: Effects pack a great deal of information into an instant, so they fly by unnoticed at full speed, yet remove them and the game looks plain. The same game can feel quite different with different effects. Careful observation is a shortcut to building them well.
how_to_apply: Add debug slow motion, a background-off toggle and on/off toggles for each display element. Record your effects and reference games' effects and step through them to see shapes, timing and layering. A/B a key scene with effects off. Give swings, punches and kicks trails or blur. Add celebratory flourishes aimed at the player who scored.
anti_pattern: Skimping on effects because they're only on screen for an instant. Judging effects only at full speed.
example: His long montage of Smash Ultimate effects in slow motion with backgrounds disabled; blade trails, without which attacks lack oomph; confetti in Ultimate's KO explosion praising the player who landed the KO.
review_question: With effects turned off, does the scene look noticeably plainer? If not, are your effects doing enough?
keywords: effects vfx slow-motion frame-by-frame study reference debug background-off juice polish celebration confetti

principle: Let each character's look express its essence and its mechanics
why: Characters must be well established, and that takes everyone assigned to one understanding its core essence and drawing it out further; it can't be done by one person. Each character should be describable in a word or two. Visual details are where that identity, and the rules behind it, become visible to the player.
how_to_apply: Write a short core-essence statement per character and share it with everyone on that character. Make effects and trails carry the move's character: an emphasized edge where a sword's tip is stronger, a frenzied trail for a heavy blade, no fade-out for a blade that emits light. Show state changes on the character's body. Let poses express personality. Where a system has hidden rules, consider an effect that shows them.
anti_pattern: A generic trail or effect shared by every character. A design that matches the reference but misses who the character is. Identity left to the planner alone.
example: Marth's tip-emphasized trail, Ike's frenzied trail, Travis's unfading beam katana; the hitstop effect that shows the knockback path a hit player can adjust; Kirby drawn slightly plumper and recolored when he holds a copy ability; copy hats that boosted Kirby's appeal.
review_question: Could a player guess what this character is about, and what its moves do best, from its look and effects alone?
keywords: character-design identity core-essence personality expression mechanics visual-language trails status cast strengths

principle: Prefer expressive exaggeration over literal realism
why: Game characters lose much of the information real people convey, and nothing in them truly exists, so 'too much' is 'just right'. Manga and anime conventions often express a character better than realism, and can even be cheaper to produce. You can't fix what you don't notice, so question inherited conventions.
how_to_apply: Exaggerate signature features and expressions past where they feel done, judged at in-game size. Try manga conventions such as a mouth on the side of the face in profile, animated by swapping cels. Use shape animation for squash and stretch through gaps. Review models at the angles players see, and question default anatomy that reads less expressively.
anti_pattern: Rejecting a technique only because it isn't realistic. Keeping an inherited modeling convention without asking whether it reads.
example: Mega Man Legends' profile mouths; Sonic's side-of-face mouth; Kirby's and Jigglypuff's Smash mouths remodeled for a more expressive profile; Wolf's damage face pushed to suit his jaw.
review_question: Where did we choose realism by default, and would an exaggerated or manga-style version read better at game size?
keywords: exaggeration stylization manga anime cartoon expression realism profile mouth squash-stretch too-much-is-just-right

principle: Size characters and targets for the screen they're played on
why: A screen covers only about 30 degrees of the player's vision, so a target of realistic size can be a speck. Tiny targets on a big screen lack impact as entertainment, and on a handheld they make players stare at a small area. Big targets also forgive beginners' slightly off-target attacks.
how_to_apply: Decide how much of the screen gameplay and targets should occupy before fixing camera and field of view. Scale enemies up if they look tiny. Make bosses in beginner games big enough that slightly off-target attacks still hit. When characters are small on screen, push their exaggeration and carry their appeal elsewhere, such as HUD portraits.
anti_pattern: Choosing a camera for realism that leaves little room for play. Pinpoint distant targets on a handheld.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's standard enemies at four or five times Pit's size; Whispy Woods made big for Kirby's newcomers; Smash HUD portraits because fighters are often small.
review_question: On the real target screen, are the things players must hit and watch big enough to read and to feel?
keywords: screen-size scale enemy-size field-of-view fov handheld targets impact beginners on-screen-size

principle: Unify mixed art styles around one visual concept
why: Artists on one team must produce the same visual style whatever their specialty, and characters imported as-is from different sources look like 'a fight between live action and animation'. The more advanced the visuals, the more unifying style costs, but it's a necessary step.
how_to_apply: Before production, have your strongest artist make a few image boards (world, scenery, characters, items) and build every model and the lighting from them. When mixing styles, meet in the middle: slightly desaturate pure primaries and make them respond to light, add material texture to flat cartoon characters and ease texture on realistic ones, tweak proportions where matchups look silly, give everyone the same refinement pass, and ground stylized features in how they'd work if the character really existed. Apply the same check to animation, effects and audio. Vet a new technique before adopting it mid-project.
anti_pattern: Each artist working in a personal style. Official designs imported unchanged. A trendy technique adopted mid-project that the staff don't know and the game doesn't suit.
example: Mario's denim overalls; Bayonetta's adjusted proportions; R.O.B.'s added detail; Donkey Kong's and Yoshi's eyelids closing instead of comic pupils; Meta Knight's mask reshaped to sit beside realistic fighters; Kirby Super Star's mid-project CG backgrounds, which didn't fit.
review_question: Lined up in one frame, do all characters and assets look like they belong to the same game?
keywords: art-direction style-unification consistency image-boards concept-art crossover mixed-styles cohesion live-action-and-animation

principle: Draw the light an asset reflects, not just the asset
why: Everything we see is light reflected into our eyes; it isn't as simple as seeing a red thing as red. A tree with a brown trunk and green leaves isn't finished, even if lighting is someone else's job. Cheap lighting techniques also let you fit more objects on screen than heavy per-object shaders would.
how_to_apply: Make lighting part of an asset's definition of done. Light groups of repeated assets with colored light, brighten the spots that would catch more light, vary hue slightly across copies, and add atmosphere that does more than flat fog. Enrich flat backgrounds with contrast and hue-shifted light. Let stylized colors respond to scene lighting. Check that character lighting on each stage isn't too dark.
anti_pattern: Calling an asset done with base colors only. Copy-pasted assets with identical color. Flat, evenly lit backgrounds. Bright primaries that look the same under any light.
example: The cut-and-pasted forest improved with colored light, sprayed highlights, hue variation and atmosphere; the Spirits cave retouch with a hue-shifted reflective glow; Hollow Bastion's character lighting brightened.
review_question: Can you tell where the light in this scene comes from and what color it is?
keywords: lighting light color hue-variation atmosphere backgrounds environment-art shading definition-of-done colored-light

principle: Judge visuals on the final composited frame at gameplay distance
why: Drawing each material's texture on its own won't create cohesive visuals. On modern hardware the post-processed frame, with blended hues and reflections, decides quality more than any single model: what matters is how everything comes together. Many problems, such as even spacing, square outlines, mismatched proportions or wrong scale, only show in the whole frame or from the gameplay camera.
how_to_apply: Approve art in the game with all post-processing on, not in a model viewer. Review scale and lighting on full screenshots. Check assets both up close and from the gameplay camera. Line up mixed characters in game rather than against their source art. Step back from details regularly. On high-end projects, give one person responsibility for post-processing and final output.
anti_pattern: Polishing props in isolation. Approving assets one at a time. Getting lost in minor details.
example: The same stage in Melee (each object its own distinct color) and Ultimate (blended hues, reflections off the water); the Mishima Dojo wall that only looked square and evenly spaced from far away; Bayonetta looks odd beside her original art but right in the game.
review_question: Was this asset approved in the final frame, at the distance and lighting players will see it?
keywords: final-output post-processing compositing framebuffer whole-image cohesion review gameplay-distance big-picture

principle: Spend detail where players actually look
why: Console hardware is weaker than people think, so you must separate major elements from minor ones. Players mostly watch the center of the screen and the playable surface, and how much an environment means depends on how closely the gameplay makes them scrutinize it. A bit of playfulness is fine if deadlines and performance hold, but detail nobody will see is waste.
how_to_apply: Rank assets by how much they're seen: the area in front of the camera and the stage surface first, off-screen foundations last. Budget each model by its on-screen size, raised for models also shown up close elsewhere. Put environment detail where cautious play makes players look, and where the camera actually reveals background. Build LOD only when the gain is worth the labor. Build stage art for the worst-case load.
anti_pattern: Turning car tires deep in a backdrop. Over-investing in elements that are tiny on screen. Detail spread evenly regardless of attention.
example: Smash skyspheres detailed in front of the camera; the Inkling stage's turning backdrop tires toned down; Dark Souls' frequent deaths making players scrutinize every nook, versus the same art at Sonic's speed; Ultimate's stages built to hold 60 fps with eight fighters.
review_question: Is the most detail where the player's eyes actually spend time during play?
keywords: budget optimization lod detail-allocation major-minor performance screen-center environment-art presence

principle: Raise graphics and gameplay together, because graphics multiply fun
why: Environments are massless mirages until gameplay gives them presence: a game where you die often makes players scrutinize every corner. In the other direction, on crowded storefronts a banner decides whether anyone looks at your game, so visuals that don't draw players in mean nobody plays. Calling visuals irrelevant to gameplay won't matter if nobody buys the game.
how_to_apply: Build environment art alongside the mechanics and match its density to how closely play makes players look. Treat storefront banners and key art as critical. When readability and beauty conflict, keep both and give gameplay the slight edge.
anti_pattern: Writing graphics off as irrelevant to fun. Finishing art in isolation from how the game is played.
example: Dark Souls and Sekiro versus the same graphics at Sonic's speed; Steam banners; Smash Ultimate's roughly 115 base stages recreating the worlds of dozens of games.
review_question: Would a player scrolling a storefront stop on our key art, and does our gameplay make players look at the art we spent the most on?
keywords: graphics fun presence key-art banner storefront marketing appeal environment gameplay

principle: Direct art by showing, and approve whatever meets the goal
why: Palette, contrast, mood and shape are hard to put into words, and showing communicates more clearly than telling, especially over email. A retouch takes him about five minutes, ten at most, which beats explaining. But a retouch is direction, not final art, and his goal isn't to make everything match his own ideals.
how_to_apply: Send a quick paintover, retouched screenshot, mouse sketch, posed figure or density reference beside the original, with one line on what to change and why. Make notes concrete: which axis, which spacing, which repetition. Flag tiny flaws the moment you see them. State each asset's core goal in one sentence and approve anything that meets it. If several rounds don't converge, ship it and move on. Keep physical models of the characters for artists.
anti_pattern: Long text descriptions of visual changes. The director retouching everything. Swinging direction back and forth each round. Rejecting good work because it differs from your mental image.
example: The Spirits cave retouch (duplicate the layer, boost contrast, shift hue, erase where light hits, harmonize); the Mishima Dojo wall feedback; the hit-flash mockup; a figure posed to show Sora's forward aerial; the flame density reference for Pyra.
review_question: Does every piece of visual feedback include an image, and does each asset have a one-line goal to approve against?
keywords: art-direction supervision feedback retouch paintover mockup reference-image sketch figure review approval iteration

principle: Stage explosions as flash, blast and smoke, then let them finish
why: Spitting out a single blast of fire is tempting but flat. An instant flash tells players something intense just happened, the crisp blast is the key part, and smoke plus a natural conclusion show where it happened. For pure gameplay, clearing the smoke instantly would be better, but a shorter explosion lacks impact, so the damage window is kept short while the visuals run their course.
how_to_apply: Open with an instant flash whose light rays reach well past the blast radius, mixed with black elements, plus a shockwave and a flare. Follow with a crisp roar of flames from the center with sparks. Keep the hitbox active for only part of the blast. Let black smoke take over as the flames wane, and end with flickering sparkles. Add a screen flash or shake only where it suits that explosion. Make ground variants whose blast spreads upward and whose shockwave follows the floor.
anti_pattern: One fire sprite for the whole explosion. A pure white flash that disappears on white backgrounds. Cutting the explosion short. A hitbox that lasts as long as the visuals.
example: Star Force's five-frame explosion (flash to smoke to gone); Smash's standard explosion; Young Link's bomb on the ground; extra smoke added so Sora's Final Smash explosion reads; slight gusts of wind around Smash explosions.
review_question: Does each explosion have a distinct flash, blast, smoke and ending, with a hit window shorter than the visual?
keywords: explosion explosions flash blast smoke shockwave flare sparks phases vfx bombs screen-flash ground-variant

principle: Sell scale through materials, saturation, atmosphere and density, not shape
why: A huge object and its plastic model share shape and color, and CG objects naturally look like scale models: more saturated, glossier, less affected by ambient light, flatter in material. Big things looking small is the usual failure. Shallow depth of field and high saturation are exactly the tricks that make photos look miniature. Effects suffer the same way: a big flame without density reads as a candle.
how_to_apply: Fix materials before shape: enlarge texture loops and painted detail, lower saturation on realistic assets, shrink gloss area and strength, match normal-map detail to real size, add dirt and mixed hues to big mechanical or monotone surfaces. Lower saturation and add haze with distance, so the nearest objects are the most saturated. Avoid depth-of-field blur. Give large effects more loops or smaller particles. Use placement and surroundings to establish size.
anti_pattern: Small texture loops, oversaturated or glossy large objects, normal maps at the wrong scale. Full saturation on distant giants. Big flames built from a few large shapes.
example: Off-color tile spots and grass hue variation that betray a small object; the miniature photo trick (blur top and bottom, raise saturation, cut blue); Pyra's sword flames given a density reference because they looked like a candle.
review_question: Viewed in-scene from gameplay distance, does each large object or effect read as huge, or as a toy?
keywords: scale sense-of-scale miniature saturation gloss specular texture-loop normal-map aerial-perspective haze depth-of-field density

principle: Honor the source's feeling instead of copying it literally
why: An exact copy of one reference can match and still feel wrong, because what fans love is a feeling. He wants to 'honor the feeling and do what works best', which sometimes means moving closer to the original and sometimes mixing in newer details. In licensed work, faithfulness and satisfying fans' love come first.
how_to_apply: Get original production material and put source screenshots next to your version. Compare palette, saturation, relative brightness of costume parts, eye shape and signature poses. Combine the classic design with selected newer details. Stay close where the source shows a lot and invent where it shows little. Don't invent facial range the source lacks; carry emotion through movement instead. Get the rights holder's permission for changes.
anti_pattern: Matching one source version exactly but missing the character. Freely rewriting an established character. Inventing expressions that contradict the source.
example: The Mii Nakoruru costume revised from a literal KOF XIV match; Kazuya's knockdown pose and Final Smash moved toward his original game; CG shots pushed toward FFVII: Advent Children, starting by lowering saturation; Steve's only facial animation is a blink; Game & Watch LCD patterns used as reference.
review_question: Next to the original, does our version feel like the character fans remember, even where details differ?
keywords: faithfulness source-material adaptation licensed fan-service reference original crossover authenticity homage

principle: Protect players' eyes: cap glare, flashing, blur and depth of field
why: Bright glowing elements are hard on the eyes, regulations now keep flashing mild, too much blur makes it hard to tell what's going on, and trying to focus on something blurry can be physically uncomfortable. The more natural a blur, the less discomfort. Inertia-heavy camera motion makes some players sick.
how_to_apply: Raise contrast on glowing areas like magma but cap their brightness. Keep full-screen flashes brief and mild, scaled down when the camera is close. Use pre-drawn blur textures on spinning parts, keep artificial blur subtle and offer a strength option. Remove depth of field and focus pulls except where truly needed. Offer toggles for camera embellishments such as footstep shake.
anti_pattern: Searing magma or full-screen strobing. Heavy motion blur that hides the action. Depth of field everywhere as cheap atmosphere.
example: World of Light's magma kept from getting too bright; a focus shift removed from Sora's fighter reveal; the Spirit Train stage's built-in wheel and rail blur; the spinning blur he regrets leaving off Kirby Air Ride's Wheel.
review_question: After an hour of play, is anything on screen glaring, strobing, fuzzy or nauseating, and can players turn it down?
keywords: eye-strain comfort accessibility photosensitivity flashing glare motion-blur depth-of-field dof motion-sickness options

principle: Check color on matched screens and on the displays players use
why: Each monitor shows color differently, even the same model from the same maker, and room lighting changes perception; for artists and supervisors any variance is fatal. Games end up on ordinary TVs, so calibration devices only go so far. Older games were made for CRTs, whose glow and dithering look different on today's panels.
how_to_apply: Set up one shared reference screen everyone can see and calibrate monitors by eye against it. Retire monitors that crush shadows or flatten contrast. Light art areas neutrally. Check flashes and dark scenes on real LCD TVs. When porting or imitating retro art, judge it as it looked on a CRT.
anti_pattern: Assuming everyone sees the same colors. Moody tinted office lighting. Approving art on a monitor that hides shadows.
example: The Mewtwo image on two monitors, one losing the right-hand shadow; an office lit in yellow whose art came out bluish; checkered pixel patterns that read differently on a CRT.
review_question: Was this art approved on the team reference screen and checked on an ordinary TV?
keywords: color-calibration monitors color-disparity lighting reference-screen tv crt display lcd art-review

principle: Make imaginary objects feel real through weight, light, use, placement and air
why: To a creator a game world is a massless mirage; players feel it as real only because visuals, audio, programming and parameters work together, which he calls 'expression'. A regular table and a miniature have the same shape; presentation and arrangement decide which one you see. Imitating reality also packs in information: floors look hard, windups look powerful.
how_to_apply: For each prop decide texture, light response, weight, use and placement, not just shape. Add environmental wind so cloth and foliage flutter, and small gusts around explosions. Make broken things irregular (no perpendicular cuts, uneven spacing, no copy-pasted fragments) and keep debris out of the space characters move through. Do a top-down plausibility sweep: windmills turning with the wind, debris spread naturally, light shafts through broken ceilings, motion that isn't excessive.
anti_pattern: Objects that only look like the thing. Forgetting invisible forces like airflow. Manufactured-looking breakage.
example: The table and the miniature table; Smash's environmental wind; the Cloud Sea of Alrest windmills that once turned against the wind; the Mishima Dojo destructible wall.
review_question: Does every object in the scene sit and behave the way its real counterpart would, including in the wind?
keywords: expression believability physicality weight airflow wind props destruction plausibility mimicry realism

principle: Give each weapon its own trail, and fix the swing until it reads
why: Attacks lack oomph without blade trails, so getting them right has a tremendous impact. But a trail that simply traces a fast swing looks angular and can be nearly invisible from the side, so the animation usually has to change too.
how_to_apply: Build trails as a polygon ribbon swept behind the blade like a folding fan, with a translucent, fading tail. For swings that finish in one frame, show a single flat trail image and let hitstop hold it on screen. Check every swing from the gameplay camera and adjust the animation rather than using plain horizontal slashes. Design each trail for its weapon. Extend a similar blur to punches and kicks.
anti_pattern: One generic trail for every sword. Plain horizontal slashes that vanish from the side. Raw path-tracing that looks angular.
example: Lucina's standard blue trail, Marth's emphasized edge, Ike's frenzied trail, Pit's two-color trail, Pyra's flames, Travis's beam katana trail with no fade.
review_question: From the gameplay camera, does every swing leave a clear trail that says what kind of weapon it is?
keywords: blade-trails sword-trails swing-trails weapon-trails slash motion-blur ribbon vfx melee

principle: Get the most out of every particle
why: Particles always cost processing, however powerful the hardware, so his teams set rules: they must appear in the largest numbers at the lowest cost. Billboards are cheap and perfect for intangible effects like flashes of light, but look wrong from some angles. Effects are always moving, so looking quick and fierce matters more than fine detail.
how_to_apply: Keep particle lifetimes short and compensate with higher speed. Pack several particles into one billboard and draw billboards somewhat large. Stagger spawn timing across emitters and offset positions so particles don't overlap. Build flashes and particles from camera-facing billboards with sparks on top. Orbit the camera around billboarded objects and switch to models where they look odd. Use Y-axis billboards carefully. principle: On small, low-color canvases, give every pixel and color a job
why: With few colors and 16x16 sprites, every choice shows. Odd-sized shapes have a true center line, so a 15x15 circle looks rounder than a 16x16 one. A third color is best spent on edge softening or a reflection, and the background decides how well soft edges work. Art made for one display can read differently on another.
how_to_apply: Draw round or symmetric sprites at odd dimensions. See how far an outline plus one highlight carries a material before adding colors. Spend extra colors on anti-aliasing against the real background or on reflections. Mix light and dark pixels so small effects show on any background. Design emblems and shared parts that survive mirroring. When imitating retro art, remember its dithering was made for CRTs.
anti_pattern: Even-sized small circles. Mesh shading on something meant to read as round. Decorative colors with no job.
example: Kirby's 16x16 Game Boy sprite; outline plus highlight reads as a bubble, solid black plus highlight as a cannonball; the Maxim Tomato's 'M' and Dee Jay's 'MAXIMUM' pants survive mirroring; Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half.
review_question: Does every color in this sprite do a job (shape, highlight, edge, reflection), and does it still read flipped and on its real background?
